habit_line: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome, Cryptarithm Crackers! Some digits in today’s sums have gone missing, and some have been turned into letters. Like code-breakers, we will crack them one column at a time and prove our answer is the only one.
do: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: I show you a number. You write the number that makes 1000 with it. Ready? 350.
How did you work it out? Did anyone go to 400 first, then to 1000?
Can you use the digits 1 to 9, each once, to make a sum of two 3-digit numbers with a 3-digit answer? Do you think there are many ways, a few, or none?
stuck: Stuck: “Put small digits in the hundreds of the two numbers you add. Try 1 and 2 in the hundreds.” (This is also printed on the explore slide.)
Close but a digit repeats: “Swap two cards in the ones column and add again.”

Ready for more: the Go further card on the slide (find more sums; what is always true? the smallest and biggest answer). Or: “Add up the digits of your answer. Does a friend’s answer give the same total?”

say: “4A68 + 17B5 = C043. I start at the ones: 8 + 5 = 13. I write 3 and carry 1.”
“Tens: 6 + B + the carried 1 must end in 4. 6 + 7 + 1 = 14. So B is 7, and I carry 1 again.”
“Hundreds: A + 7 + 1 must end in 0, so it makes 10. A is 2. Thousands: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6, so C is 6. So 4268 + 1775 = 6043. I check by adding it all again.”
“For subtraction I turn it round: 6A02 − B35C = 1947 means 1947 + B35C = 6A02. Now I can add, column by column.”

do: Ask: “Which column did you start with? Why?”
Ask: “Is there a carry coming into this column?”
Ask: “How do you know this is the ONLY answer?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Write the carried 1 above the next column.”

say: “Why do we start at the ones column?”
“How can a puzzle have only one answer?”
ask: “Why do we start at the ones column?”

A carry moves from right to left, so the ones column is the only column with nothing coming into it. Once we know the ones, we know the carry, and then the next column has only one possible digit, and so on.

say: “Code-breakers check every column. Today you worked backwards, guessed and improved, and proved your answers.”

p3l2-title.note: Objective: Find missing digits in 4-digit addition and subtraction by working column by column from the ones; check subtraction by adding and work backwards in magic squares and number pyramids (heuristic: work backwards); use guess, check and improve for digit-card and shape puzzles (heuristic: guess and check). Materials: Digit cards 0–9 (one set per child), mini whiteboards, a printed 3 × 3 grid, counters or small paper squares to move around. Online: Children use the cut-out digit cards at the back of the workbook (or paper squares numbered 0–9) and draw the grids on paper. Share the screen for the column sums and write on them. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 25 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 25 to 34 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 34 to 39, worksheet 39 to 71 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 68 everyone chooses), talk time 71 to 79 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 79 to 85, look back 85 to 88, stamp and close 88 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it. SPINE: Today's tool is Guess and check. Make a sensible guess, check it against every clue, improve it. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p3l2-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is Guess and check. Make a sensible guess, check it against every clue, improve it. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l2-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "say it" ONCE for both: children say both answers together on three (about 30 seconds); nothing is held up to the camera. SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and say them together on three (once for both puzzles); nothing is held up to the camera. No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): A = 5. Listen for: Tens: A + 3 must make 8, so A = 5. Check: 255 + 134 = 389. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 2750. Listen for: Work backwards: take away what he won. 4000 − 1250 = 2750. Check: 2750 + 1250 = 4000. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l2-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Make 1000. Play TWO rounds of three cards: round 1 is the top row (350, 720, 105), round 2 the bottom row (999, 460, 75). Point to one card at a time; children write the missing number on their whiteboards and say the answer together on three; click to reveal. Answers: 650, 280, 895, 1, 540, 925. Ask: "How did you work out 720?" Good ways: count on to the next hundred (720 → 800 is 80) then to 1000 (200 more), so 280; or use bonds of 10 for each place. For 105 watch for 995 (it is 895: 105 + 895 = 1000). Ready for more: "Make 10 000 with 3500." (6500)

p3l2-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Mental maths, no written working. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. Ask for 2: "Which digits changed when we took away 1? Why did so many change?" (every 0 had to be exchanged). Three quick questions only. Questions 4 and 5 (8000 − 2500: 5500; 4999 + 2: 5001) are on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook.

p3l2-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 21. Pairs work with the digit cards 1 to 9 (online: paper squares). Ask them to predict first: "Many ways, a few, or none?" Each card is used once, so the nine boxes use all nine digits. Hints: "Put small digits in the hundreds of the two numbers you add, like 1 and 2." "A digit repeats? Swap two cards and add again." Two examples to keep in your pocket: 173 + 286 = 459 and 218 + 349 = 567. Pairs need about 6 to 7 minutes of work, so keep the debrief to the three questions on the next slide. Ready for more: the Go further card on the slide (find more sums; what is always true?). "Add the digits of your answer. Compare with another pair." GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): Find more sums. What is always true about the answer? What is the smallest answer? The biggest? Answer: Smallest 459 (for example 173 + 286); biggest 981 (for example 235 + 746). Every answer has digits adding to 18. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l2-explore2.note: Minutes 21 to 25. Let pairs keep working, then gather them and collect sums on the board. Answers: 1) There are many: 168, if 173 + 286 and 286 + 173 count once. 2) Exactly once, every time. 3) The digits of the answer always add up to 18 (4 + 5 + 9 = 18, 5 + 6 + 7 = 18). Do not explain why in full; just say: "Mathematicians can prove this is ALWAYS true. Notice it, test it, explain why!" Anyone ready for more: "Can the answer be less than 400?" (No: the smallest answer is 459.)

p3l2-teach1.note: Teach. Click once for each step; the solved sum fades in over the puzzle, then the answer. Think-aloud: "I start at the ones, because nothing is carried into the ones. 8 + 5 = 13. I write 3 and carry 1. Tens: 6 + B + the carried 1 must end in 4. 6 + 1 is 7, and 7 + 7 = 14, so B is 7 and I carry 1 again. Hundreds: A + 7 + 1 must end in 0, so it makes 10: A is 2. Thousands: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6." Ask: "Why not start at the thousands?" (we do not know yet if something is carried into it).

p3l2-try1.note: Whiteboards. a) Ones 5 + B ends in 1, so 5 + 6 = 11, B = 6, carry 1. Tens A + 4 + 1 ends in 2, so A = 7. Hundreds 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 ✓. b) 6 + D ends in 3: 6 + 7 = 13, D = 7. Tens C + 5 + 1 = 12, so C = 6. c) is a preview of the next slide: turn it round, 296 + B58 = 6A4. Ones 6 + 8 = 14, carry 1. Tens 9 + 5 + 1 = 15, so A = 5, carry 1. Hundreds 2 + B + 1 = 6, so B = 3.

p3l2-teach2.note: Teach the heuristic WORK BACKWARDS: subtraction and addition undo each other. Click 1 turns the subtraction into an addition (the picture changes). Think-aloud: "Subtracting with missing digits on top is hard, because I would have to exchange without knowing the digit. So I undo it: the answer plus the number taken away gives back the first number." Common error: looking for a digit that can be taken from 2 to leave 7. There is none; it must be 12 − 5 = 7.

p3l2-teach3.note: Teach the heuristic GUESS AND CHECK, then IMPROVE. Click for each row and note. Think-aloud: "First guess 43 − 21 = 22. Can I do better? The tens make the biggest difference, so the tens digits should be next to each other, like 3 and 2." Row 2: 42 − 31 = 11, better. Row 3: try the tens 3 and 2 with the ones swapped round. "Now the bigger number, 3_, should have the smallest ones digit left, 1, and the smaller number, 2_, the biggest, 4: 31 − 24 = 7." Check other pairs quickly: 41 − 32 = 9, 21 − 14 is not allowed (1 twice). So 7 is the smallest. If there is a moment, ask orally (no slide): cards 1, 2, 3, 4, the greatest sum (73, for example 41 + 32) and the smallest sum (37, for example 13 + 24).

p3l2-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Forgetting the carried 1 when working out the missing digit in the next column. (2) In subtraction, looking for a digit that can be taken from 3 to leave 8 (there is none) instead of regrouping: 13 − 5 = 8. (3) Magic squares: guessing numbers instead of finding a full line first to get the total.

p3l2-break.note: Five minutes. Try 3, 8, 0, 5, 2. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l2-teachmagic.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3, the magic square). This is WORK BACKWARDS again: we know the total, so we take away to find the missing number. Click order: step 1, diagonals appear, step 2, the rest appear, step 3, check. Ask: "Which line should we use next? One with only ONE gap." Do not show the worksheet square.

p3l2-ws1.note: Minutes 41.5 to 54.5. Walk around. Ask "Which column did you start with?" and "Is there a carry coming in?" Q2(c), the smallest difference, is a take-home question (starred in the workbook): do not spend lesson time on it; the idea is taught on the guess-check-improve slide. Expect several tries on (a) and (b); praise improving a guess. PAGE 1 CLOCK (41.5 to 54.5): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 9.5 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l2-ws1ans.note: Self-check. Q1a: ones 7 + 8 = 15, carry 1; tens 4 + the missing digit + 1 ends in 2, so 7 (12), carry 1; hundreds the missing digit + 5 + 1 ends in 0, so 4, carry 1; thousands 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Q1b: turn it round, 316 + 216 = 532: ones 6 + 6 = 12, carry 1; tens 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so the missing digit is 3; hundreds 3 + 2 = 5. Q2a: big digits in the hundreds (6, 5), then tens (4, 3), then ones (2, 1). Q2c: hundreds 4 and 3 (next to each other); 4 gets the smallest ones left (1, 2), 3 gets the biggest (6, 5): 412 − 365 = 47. It is the only way to get 47. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l2-teachpyr.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Click through: step, picture, step, step, picture, check. Stress "undo the adding by taking away". For Q4b (equal corner bricks) say only: "If you are stuck, guess a number for the corners, check the top, then improve your guess."

p3l2-teach999.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Ask: "Why is 999 − 372 so easy?" (9 is the biggest digit, so we never need to exchange). Check: 628 + 372 = 1000. Your turn: 999 − 456 = 543, plus 1 = 544. Q5 asks children to notice the same pattern with 9999, so do not show 4-digit examples.

p3l2-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Q6 hint if needed: "Three of the same digit add up to a number that ends in that same digit. Which digits can do that?"

p3l2-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q3: total 1200 + 1700 + 1600 = 4500; diagonals give 1800 and 1400; then 1900, 1100, 1300. Q4a: 5975 − 3600 = 2375, 2375 − 1250 = 1125, 3600 − 1125 = 2475. Q4b: corners equal; middle bricks are corner + 2000 each; top 7000, so each middle brick is 3500 and each corner 1500. Q6: B + B + B ends in B, so B is 0 or 5. If B = 5, the tens get a carry of 1 and A + A + A + 1 cannot end in A (try them). So B = 0; then A + A + A ends in A, A is not 0, so A = 5 and 15 gives C = 1. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l2-stretch.note: Answers: 1) A = 8, B = 9: 89 + 9 = 98 (the answer is bigger than the first number by only B, so the tens go up by 1: B = A + 1; ones: B + B = 10 + A; try A = 8). 2) 6254 and 6257 (10 000 is 1 more than 9999, so 1 more than 6253; 10 003 is 4 more than 9999, so 4 more than 6253. Check: 6254 + 3746 = 10 000). 3) A = 9, B = 2, C = 1: 99 + 22 = 121 (C must be 1; ones A + B ends in 1, so they make 11; tens 11 + 1 = 12, so B = 2 and A = 9).

p3l2-challenge.note: SUPPORT FOR Q6 (if time; this replaces the old letter-puzzle teaching slide), only for children who choose it. Model: "What do I know for sure?" AB + BA = CAC: two 2-digit numbers make less than 200, so C = 1. Ones: B + A ends in 1, so B + A = 11, carry 1. Tens: A + B + 1 = 12, and the middle digit of the answer is A, so A = 2 and B = 9: 29 + 92 = 121. For Q6 itself (AB + AB + AB = CAB) the idea is the same: start with what the ones digit must be. GO FURTHER: pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 247: 5123 − 4876 (the only way to get 247). 2) A = 4, B = 5, C = 9: 459 + 495 = 954 (the only answer).

p3l2-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? Where should we start? Q1: "Which place makes the biggest difference?" Q2: "Look at the tens column: B and C make B again. What must C be?"

p3l2-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the thousands decide most of the difference, so make them next to each other; then make the bigger number as small as it can be and the smaller number as big as it can be. Trying every neighbouring pair: 2345 − 1876 = 469, 3145 − 2876 = 269, 4125 − 3876 = 249, 5123 − 4876 = 247, 6123 − 5874 = 249, 7123 − 6854 = 269, 8123 − 7654 = 469. Q2: C cannot be 0 (the answer would start with 0), so C + carry = 10 means C = 9. Then the hundreds give A = 4 (4 + 4 + 1 = 9) and the ones give 9 + 5 = 14.

p3l2-skill1.note: Optional slide for pairs who finish early or ask for more. Show it only on request and never announce who is working on it. Children write the answer on their own paper and say it together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Answers and tutor lines are for you only. Item 1 (Pairing: make tens and hundreds; tool of the day idea: Try something simpler). SAY: "Do not add left to right. Hunt for partners." ASK: "Which numbers are partners? How did you find the partner of 260?" LISTEN FOR: "260 + 140 = 400, because 60 + 40 = 100." ANSWER: a) 8 + 2, 7 + 3, 6 + 4 and 9 + 1 each make 10, so 40. b) 260 + 140 = 400, 380 + 120 = 500, 410 + 90 = 500, so 1400. Item 2 (Series sums: first plus last; tool of the day idea: Spot the pattern). SAY: "Write the list twice: forwards, then backwards underneath." ASK: "What is the second number plus the second last? What do you notice?" LISTEN FOR: "Every pair makes 55." ANSWER: a) 3 + 52 = 55. b) 4 pairs (8 numbers). c) 4 x 55 = 220.

p3l2-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: a carry moves from right to left, so the ones column is the only one with nothing coming into it. Once we know the ones, we know the carry, and the next column has only one possible digit, and so on. That is also why each puzzle has only one answer. Follow-up: "How did checking by adding help you?" Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l2-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 563 + 126 = 689 (the digit in the box is 6). Ones 3 + 6 = 9; tens: box + 2 = 8, so the box is 6; hundreds 5 + 1 = 6. Extension: find three sums of two 3-digit numbers with a 3-digit answer that use the digits 1 to 9 once each; add the digits of each answer (always 18). Answers stay on the child’s own paper and are ticked against the answer slide. Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l2-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85 to 88. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
